newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec ambivalent one year after separation vote.
newsitem.headline: Quebec ambivalent one year after separation vote.

text.p: One year after a hard-fought referendum in which it voted narrowly to stay in Canada, the French-speaking province of Quebec remains uncertain of its future as it grapples with the repercussions of the vote.

The province of 7.1 million people is struggling with a sluggish economy, a 12.6 percent unemployment rate, deep cuts in government programmes and renewed tensions between its French and English-speaking residents.

Amid a slight waning of nationalist fervor, Quebec's separatist government is preparing for the next referendum on secession. That vote may be at least two years off and will follow elections at the national and provincial levels.
Lingering political and economic uncertainty weighs heavily on a population known for its dynamism and willingness to embrace change.

"The psychological pressure is such that when we survey people we find them stressed out. It's eating away at the best of what we are," said Jean-Marc Leger, head of polling agency Groupe Leger & Leger Inc.

On Oct. 30, 1995, 4.5 million of Quebec's 5.1 million eligible voters cast ballots in a referendum on whether the province should secede from Canada and seek some form of economic or political partnership with the country. The razor-thin loss by separatists -- 49.4 percent to 50.6 percent -- dismayed those who hoped to turn the province into an independent country.

In his concession speech, embittered Quebec Premier Jacques Parizeau blamed the loss on "money and the ethnic vote." He resigned soon afterward and was replaced by the charismatic Lucien Bouchard, who was credited with the strong separatist showing in the referendum.

The close result shocked Canadians who saw their 128-year-old country, the world's second largest in land area, teeter on the brink of breakup. Most shaken were Quebec's estimated 800,000 English-speakers, most of whom live in or near Montreal.

"There is definitely a cloud hanging over the province. People are uneasy, especially with the uncertainty of whether the country will stay together or not," said anglophone Montreal lawyer Frank Tutino, 41.
The surly mood worsened in the spring when ultra-nationalist members of the ruling Parti Quebecois pressed Bouchard to reinstate a law disallowing the use of English on commercial signs.

Bouchard resisted, but not before a strong backlash from English speakers, some of whom called for partition of an independent Quebec to let regions that voted against sovereignty remain in Canada. That scenario would leave the separatists with a rump of a country that would exclude Montreal -- Quebec's metropolis -- and vast tracts of the province's resource-rich north.
Meanwhile, the federal government has appealed to the Canadian Supreme Court for a ruling on Quebec's right to declare independence unilaterally.

As a hard winter of government cuts approaches, Quebeckers seem to be running out of patience for acrimonious rhetoric on both sides of the separation issue. Avril Benoit, host of a fiery open-line talk show on Montreal English-language radio station CJAD, said the "angry anglo" backlash and outbursts by fervent separatists may have reached a saturation point.

"You can't be in such a state of high alert, on the lookout for a future referendum for more than a limited period of time," she said. She voiced hope that attention would shift to Quebec's economic and social problems.
Those issues dominate Premier Bouchard's agenda. On Wednesday, the first anniversary of the referendum, he will open a three-day government conference on the economy.
